analyst:
Santa Clara enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament picture at 26-8 overall after reaching the WCC tournament final, and the Broncos finished 15-3 in West Coast Conference regular-season play, a program record for league wins. The regular season ended at 24-7 before neutral-site wins over Pacific and Saint Mary’s pushed the total to 26 victories. Herb Sendek’s team finished third in the WCC standings but played like a high-end at-large team late, with the school noting an 83.8 points-per-game season average and 87.2 points per game in conference games. Santa Clara’s own pre-tournament notes also stated the Broncos were No. 42 in NET and No. 37 at KenPom entering the WCC semifinals. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-broncos-ready-to-begin-wcc-championship-journey-in-sundays-quarterfinal.aspx))

Offensively, Santa Clara is a modern spacing-and-pace team built around volume threes, offensive rebounding, and multiple scoring guards rather than a single dominant isolation star. The clearest tendency is early-clock three-point hunting: in the March 8 WCC quarterfinal against Pacific, Santa Clara opened 6-of-9 from three and built a 24-14 lead before the under-12 timeout, then tied its WCC tournament record with 15 made threes in a 76-68 win. In the Feb. 21 win at San Francisco, the Broncos started 4-of-7 from deep, hit 13 threes overall, and used an 11-0 run keyed by quick triples to break the game open. Against Oregon State on Feb. 28, they made 13 more threes and handed out 22 assists in a 93-72 win, which is a strong indicator of drive-and-kick and inside-out ball movement rather than stagnant offense. Specific lineup usage supports that: Sash Gavalyugov is a bench microwave shooter, hitting 5-of-9 from three for 21 points against Seattle U. on Feb. 11, while Allen Graves gives them a small-ball frontcourt scorer who can pop or attack closeouts, as shown by his 30 points and 13 rebounds at Washington State on Feb. 7. Santa Clara also uses second-half pressure points to create tempo offense; in the USF win it scored 25 points off 17 turnovers and added 12 offensive rebounds. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/3/8/mens-basketball-broncos-punch-ticket-to-wcc-championship-semifinal.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The half-court scheme is not just random spread ball. Santa Clara repeatedly plays through slot ball screens and flare actions to free Hammond, Mahi, and Gavalyugov for catch-and-shoot threes or downhill attacks. The evidence is in who gets shots and how scoring runs form. In the Jan. 17 win over Saint Mary’s, Thierry Darlan stopped a 12-0 Gaels run with a key basket, then Gavalyugov and Bukky Oboye scored off quick-trigger actions that restored control. In the Feb. 14 Gonzaga game, Santa Clara regained the lead in the second half with back-to-back threes from Darlan and Gavalyugov to make it 60-55, showing how Sendek uses weak-side shooters after initial paint touches. Jake Ensminger’s seven assists against Oregon State and four assists in Gavalyugov’s 37-point explosion against LMU on Jan. 10 also point to a connective-forward role at 6-foot-9, often facilitating from the elbow or top. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-broncos-hold-off-saint-marys-to-remain-undefeated-at-home.aspx))

Defensively, Santa Clara is more disruptive than purely conservative. The Broncos lead with activity at the point of attack, heavy dig help, and aggressive hands that feed transition chances. They had 14 steals against San Francisco on Feb. 21 and scored 25 points off turnovers; Mahi had four steals, Darlan had four steals, and Knapper had three. Against Saint Mary’s on Jan. 17, they held the Gaels to 32 percent shooting and 4-of-22 from three while holding them scoreless for the first seven minutes of the second half. That game is the cleanest snapshot of their defensive ceiling: gap help into the lane, hard closeouts to the arc, and enough rebounding to finish possessions. The downside is that elite frontcourts can punish them if the first layer breaks. Gonzaga shot 56 percent in the Feb. 14 94-86 win in Santa Clara and 52.8 percent in the WCC title game on March 10, while Saint Mary’s hit Santa Clara for 86 points in Moraga on Feb. 25. So the profile is clear: Santa Clara can generate steals and speed teams up, but against disciplined, physical offenses their interior resistance is less reliable. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/2/21/broncos-set-program-record-for-conference-wins-with-94-73-triumph-against-san-francisco.aspx))

Sendek’s coaching philosophy is visible in the game-to-game adjustment history. He is still a structure coach: he values ball security, layered spacing, and lineup versatility, but this year’s group plays faster and shoots more threes than some earlier Sendek teams. The documented adjustment arc is strong. After losing 89-77 at Gonzaga on Jan. 8, where a 20-2 second-half Bulldog run decided the game, Santa Clara later pushed Gonzaga again on Feb. 14, leading 60-55 with 12:24 left before losing 94-86. That progression showed improved offensive comfort against Gonzaga’s size. Against Saint Mary’s, Santa Clara first won a half-court grinder 62-54 on Jan. 17 by choking off the Gaels’ shooting, then got blown out 86-67 in Moraga on Feb. 25 when Saint Mary’s dictated terms, then beat the Gaels 76-71 in the WCC semifinal on March 9 in a game with 14 lead changes and six ties. That third meeting is the best evidence of Sendek’s adaptability: Santa Clara survived a possession game and closed with late-shot-clock execution rather than needing a track meet. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/1/8/mens-basketball-second-half-run-spoils-broncos-upset-bid-in-spokane.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Clutch and late-game execution is good enough to trust, though not flawless. The best example is March 9 against No. 21 Saint Mary’s: Santa Clara won 76-71, and with the Broncos leading 73-71, Gavalyugov drilled a late-shot-clock three with 13 seconds left to effectively end it. On Dec. 30 at Portland, Santa Clara won 92-85 after the Pilots tied the game with 3:21 left; Knapper then made a steal, drew a foul on the break, hit both free throws, and Mahi scored on the next possession to push the lead to 88-83 with just over a minute remaining. On Feb. 7 at Washington State, Graves made his final two free throws in the last minute of a 96-92 road win. There are also losses that reveal the ceiling: on Feb. 14 against Gonzaga, Santa Clara cut it to 73-70 with 5:47 left but got answered by a 10-4 Gonzaga run; in the March 10 WCC final, the Broncos led for 23 minutes before Gonzaga’s 50-35 second half flipped the game. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/3/10/mens-basketball-broncos-take-down-no-21-gaels-to-advance-to-wcc-championship-final.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The key players start with Christian Hammond, the lead perimeter scorer and tone-setter. Santa Clara’s Feb. 3 game notes listed Hammond at 16.8 points per game in conference play, and he repeatedly delivered star turns: 25 points in the Jan. 17 win over Saint Mary’s, 18 points against San Francisco on Feb. 21, and 24 points in the WCC final loss to Gonzaga. Elijah Mahi is the second primary scorer at 14.3 points per game in those same Feb. 3 notes. He erupted for a career-high 30 points, seven rebounds, four steals, two assists, and a block in the 94-73 win at San Francisco on Feb. 21, and he scored 19 in the March 9 semifinal win over Saint Mary’s. Allen Graves is the matchup changer: the March 11 release listed him at 11.6 points, 6.5 rebounds, 2.0 steals, and 0.9 blocks per game, and he won both WCC Freshman of the Year and Sixth Man of the Year. His best game was 30 points and 13 rebounds at Washington State on Feb. 7, and the same release says he scored in double figures 25 times. Gavalyugov is the swing shooter; he scored a career-high 37 points in the 103-72 rout of LMU on Jan. 10, 21 against Seattle U. on Feb. 11, and 23 in the WCC semifinal over Saint Mary’s. Ensminger is the glue piece, with 10 rebounds and seven assists against Oregon State on Feb. 28 and a key connective role in ball movement. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/2/3/mens-basketball-broncos-going-for-seventh-straight-wednesday-evening-in-stockton.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Notable wins define Santa Clara as a dangerous tournament team. The Jan. 17 62-54 win over Saint Mary’s proved they can win a rock fight by holding a high-level offense to 32 percent shooting. The Feb. 7 96-92 win at Washington State showed road toughness and frontcourt scoring through Graves’ 30-point, 13-rebound double-double. The Feb. 21 94-73 blowout at San Francisco revealed how devastating they are when turnovers fuel their spacing game; 14 steals, 13 made threes, and a 38-23 rebounding edge is domination. The March 9 76-71 WCC semifinal win over No. 21 Saint Mary’s is the best résumé line because it combined shot-making, poise, and late execution in a tournament setting. The losses are equally informative. The Jan. 8 loss at Gonzaga and the Feb. 14 home loss to Gonzaga showed that elite size and second-half shot-making can wear down Santa Clara’s defense. The Feb. 25 86-67 loss at Saint Mary’s showed the Broncos are more vulnerable when they lose the physical battle early; the Gaels opened 11-2 and controlled the environment. The March 10 WCC final loss to Gonzaga showed Santa Clara can compete above seed line for 20-plus minutes, but sustaining that over 40 against a top-15 caliber opponent remains difficult. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-broncos-hold-off-saint-marys-to-remain-undefeated-at-home.aspx))

As for Sendek’s NCAA tournament history, he is a veteran with deep March experience. His official Santa Clara bio and school materials identify this as his 32nd season as a Division I head coach, and his career includes multiple NCAA runs before Santa Clara. Most notably, he took NC State to the Elite Eight in 2005, and he reached the NCAA Tournament five straight times at Arizona State from 2008-09 through 2012-13, with the Sun Devils advancing to the second round in 2009 and 2014-era format equivalents otherwise ending early. At Miami (Ohio), he took the RedHawks to the NCAA Tournament in 1995 and 1997. Santa Clara has not been in the NCAA Tournament since 1996, so this 2026 team is trying to give Sendek his first Bronco NCAA appearance, but his personal history is that of a coach who has reached the field multiple times and has one documented Elite Eight run on his résumé. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-broncos-ready-to-begin-wcc-championship-journey-in-sundays-quarterfinal.aspx?utm_source=openai))
forecaster:
Santa Clara enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament discussion as a metrics-friendly team whose profile is stronger than casual perception would suggest. The Broncos finished 26-8 overall and 15-3 in WCC play, averaging 82.9 points per game while allowing 72.4. Their raw scoring margin of +10.5 points per game already signals tournament-caliber strength, but the more revealing point is that multiple rating systems place them comfortably inside the national top 50 and, in some cases, higher than that. Santa Clara was listed at No. 35 in an updated March 18, 2026 KenPom ranking table, with the Broncos carrying the 23rd-ranked offense and 82nd-ranked defense in that snapshot. A January 27 opposing game-notes packet from San Francisco listed Santa Clara at NET No. 45, KenPom No. 43, and Bart Torvik No. 34 at that point in the season, which is consistent with the idea that this team spent most of the back half of the year in the at-large conversation range rather than as a fringe mid-major curiosity. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Exact adjusted efficiencies are not broadly accessible from the major subscription models in the open web, but publicly available advanced-stat pages still give a strong baseline. Fox Sports lists Santa Clara with a 121.5 offensive rating, 103.4 defensive rating, and +18.1 net rating, with a pace of 68.8 possessions per game. Those are not opponent-adjusted KenPom numbers, but they are directionally useful: they describe a team that scores at a high-major level, plays at a moderate-to-brisk tempo, and wins primarily by offensive pressure rather than by elite shutdown defense. The offensive side is the carrying trait. KenPom’s offense rank in the low 20s paired with a defense outside the top 80 implies a classic imbalance: Santa Clara looks more dangerous as a game-by-game upset threat than as a clean six-game title formula team. ([foxsports.com](https://www.foxsports.com/college-basketball/santa-clara-broncos-team-summary-stats?category=advanced&season=2025&seasonType=reg&sort=defrtg&sortOrder=desc))

The shot-profile data reinforces that read. From Santa Clara’s official cumulative stats, the Broncos shot 46.8% from the field, 34.6% from three, and 73.6% from the foul line over 34 games. They made 344 threes on 994 attempts, which works out to a 3-point attempt rate of 45.1% of all field-goal attempts. Their derived effective field-goal percentage is 54.6%, and their derived turnover rate is 13.1%, both strong offensive markers. Free-throw rate comes in at 0.252 free-throw attempts per field-goal attempt. Santa Clara also averaged 10.1 made threes per game, a volume signal that matches the WCC note identifying them as one of the league’s leaders in three-point makes. In practical terms, this is an offense built on spacing, ball security, and enough perimeter volume to create variance in its favor. They are not purely a bombs-away team, but they absolutely lean into the three. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

On the defensive end, the profile is more mixed. Opponents shot 45.1% from the field and 32.7% from three against Santa Clara. Derived opponent eFG% was 51.3%, and opponents posted a very high free-throw rate of 0.376, which is a real stress point. Santa Clara did force turnovers well enough; opponents committed 478 turnovers, and the derived opponent turnover rate was 17.8%, while San Francisco’s January game notes also credited the Broncos with leading the WCC in steals and turnovers forced during conference play. So the defense has an identity, but it is not a clean one. It creates disruption, yet it also gives away too many whistles and too many clean interior possessions when the first line is beaten. That helps explain why the eye test may oscillate between “aggressive, athletic, dangerous” and “too loose defensively.” Both views are supported by the numbers. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Recent form is good enough to matter. Over the final 10 games listed before Selection Sunday, Santa Clara went 8-2, with wins over Washington State, San Francisco twice, Oregon State, Pacific, and Saint Mary’s in the WCC tournament before falling to Gonzaga. In those 10 games they averaged 82.8 points, essentially matching their full-season scoring average, but the more important detail is opponent quality: this was not empty stat-padding against the bottom of the league. They beat Saint Mary’s on March 9, 2026 and had also beaten Saint Mary’s on January 17, while splitting competitive games with Gonzaga and repeatedly handling the league’s middle tier by margin. A notable sign of offensive reliability is that in that closing stretch they scored 84, 86, 94, 93, 76, and 76 in six of the 10 contests, even while facing several of the WCC’s better defenses. The trend line is not explosive improvement so much as sustained top-40 caliber offense with enough defensive activity to keep the floor high. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Strength of schedule is harder to pin down exactly from open sources, but the schedule itself suggests Santa Clara was tested more than a typical mid-major. They played Xavier, Nevada, Minnesota, New Mexico, Arizona State, North Texas, Loyola Chicago, Gonzaga twice in the regular season, Saint Mary’s multiple times, and then added postseason games against Saint Mary’s and Gonzaga. That is not an inflated record built entirely on sub-200 opposition. The absence of a clean publicly visible SOS number prevents a precise rank here, but the surrounding evidence points to a schedule strong enough to validate the efficiency profile. The Broncos’ ranking band across KenPom, Torvik, and NET also indirectly confirms that the committee-facing résumé metrics did not view them as a hollow compiler. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Where do the numbers diverge from conventional wisdom? First, Santa Clara may be better offensively than many viewers assume from the WCC label alone. A top-25 KenPom offense is not decorative; it is the profile of a team that can score with real tournament opposition. Second, the Broncos are less balanced than a 26-8 record might imply. The defense is functional, disruptive, and good enough to support winning, but it does not grade like the defense of a typical protected seed. Third, their style is more modern and analytically coherent than the eye test sometimes captures: high three-point rate, low turnover rate, solid eFG%, and enough pace to create possessions. The risk is equally clear. If the perimeter shot creation stalls or if foul pressure mounts against a physically stronger front line, the underlying defensive slippage becomes much harder to hide. Netting it out, Santa Clara looks like a team whose statistical profile says “credible tournament team, dangerous draw, offense-first, upset-capable,” even if the public conversation tends to underrate them because of conference brand and because their defense does not pop in the same way as their offense. ([cleatz.com](https://cleatz.com/latest-kenpom-rankings/))
matchup-analyst:
Santa Clara enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 26-8 team that wins with efficient half-court offense, multiple ballhandlers, strong wing scoring, and unusually low self-inflicted mistakes. Their team offense produced 82.9 points per game with a 118.9 offensive rating, while the Broncos also posted just 10.8 turnovers per game against 16.8 assists, a strong 1.5 assist/turnover ratio, and 17.8 points off turnovers created on the other end. Their core production is spread across Christian Hammond (15.8 ppg, 49.0 FG%, 40.0 3PT), Elijah Mahi (13.9 ppg), Allen Graves (11.6 ppg, 6.5 rpg, 41.6 3PT), and Bukky Oboye (8.0 ppg, 66.5 FG%). That profile says Santa Clara is not purely isolation-based; it is a shared-possession offense with four credible scorers and a connective passer in Jake Ensminger, who led or co-led the team in assists in multiple games and is listed at 6-9. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/santa-clara/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Style-wise, Santa Clara wants to play with offensive flow, not chaos. The Broncos are at their best when they can run secondary break into early offense, then flatten you with drive-kick or inside-out actions from size-skilled lineups. The evidence is in their high-end scoring games: 104-73 at LMU on January 31, 103-72 vs. LMU on January 10, 98-70 vs. San Diego on January 4, 98-83 vs. Nevada on November 15, 96-92 at Washington State on February 7, and 94-73 at San Francisco on February 21. In those games, Santa Clara repeatedly hit efficient scoring thresholds rather than grinding out possessions. They also reached 12 or more made threes in numerous outings; the season high was 16 against Minnesota on November 28, and the program site noted 15 games with 10 or more threes by January 28. The clearest tactical disruptors are ball pressure that forces them later into the clock, rim protection that neutralizes Oboye’s interior efficiency, and physical closeouts that take away clean catch-and-shoot rhythm from Hammond and Graves. Their losses support that. New Mexico beat them 98-71 on December 6 while holding Santa Clara to 37.7% overall and just 22.7% from three on 44 attempts; Saint Mary’s beat them 86-67 on February 25; Gonzaga beat them three times, including 89-77 on January 8, 94-86 on February 14, and 79-68 in the WCC title game on March 10. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2541/santa-clara-broncos))

On press vulnerability: the best available season evidence suggests Santa Clara is relatively press-resistant in aggregate, because 10.8 turnovers per game is low and they finished plus-110 in turnover margin over the season, forcing 14.1 per game while committing only 10.8. That said, the named games where pressure/disruption clearly dented their offensive rhythm are North Texas on December 17 and San Diego on January 24, the two games in which Santa Clara hit its season high of 21 turnovers. Santa Clara escaped both, beating North Texas 63-60 and San Diego 85-73, but those are the strongest game-level indicators that extended ball pressure and denial can make them uncomfortable. Against better pressure teams with stronger talent, that turnover spike is much more dangerous. Because the turnover count rose but the Broncos still won, the actionable conclusion is not that they collapse versus pressure, but that you need pressure plus finishing power on the other end. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

On zone vulnerability: direct possession-type data is limited from public sources, so this is an inference from game outcomes and shot profiles rather than a charted Synergy split. Santa Clara is built to punish bad zone with spacing and shooting; 36.7% from three as a team and multiple wings above or near 40% make passive zone a bad idea. But compact, physical zone looks that force them into volume jump shooting without paint touches have worked better. The best evidence is New Mexico: Santa Clara took 44 threes, made only 10, and scored just 71 in a 27-point loss on December 6. Saint Mary’s also held them to 62 on January 17 in a Santa Clara win and to 67 in Moraga on February 25 in a Santa Clara loss, showing that disciplined shell defense and rebounding can drag them into a lower-efficiency game. So the vulnerability is not “zone” in the abstract; it is a loaded-help scheme that sits on the lane, makes Oboye a finisher not a creator, and contests Hammond/Graves above the break. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Preferred pace: Santa Clara clearly prefers games played in the 70s to 90s, where their skill depth and shooting volume show up. Their scoring résumé is full of high-possession wins: 102 at Oregon State, 104 at LMU, 103 vs. LMU, 98 vs. Nevada, 98 vs. San Diego, 96 at Washington State, 94 at San Francisco, 93 vs. Oregon State, and 92 at Portland. To force the opposite, you need to make them defend deep into possessions, dominate defensive glass to eliminate runouts, and turn their early-clock threes into late-clock drives against size. Saint Mary’s provided the clearest blueprint in the 86-67 win on February 25, and Gonzaga’s three wins also show that elite offense can flip Santa Clara into reactive defense when the Broncos cannot control tempo. Santa Clara can survive ugly games, as shown by 63-60 over North Texas and 62-54 over Saint Mary’s on January 17, but those were wins at home or in favorable contexts; over 40 minutes against a tournament-caliber opponent, the more you slow them and make every action guarded, the less comfortable they look. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2541/santa-clara-broncos))

Size and athleticism by position: at point/lead-guard, Santa Clara often relies on Christian Hammond (6-4) and Sash Gavalyugov (6-3), so they usually have size versus small backcourts but can be challenged by elite speed guards who can turn the corner repeatedly. At the wing, Mahi is 6-7, Graves is a strong rebounder from the perimeter, KJ Cochran is 6-5, and Gehrig Normand is 6-6; that gives Santa Clara real positional size at the 2/3/4 slots. Ensminger is a 6-9 guard/forward connector, which is a mismatch creator offensively against smaller second units. Oboye gives them a 6-8 interior finisher, while freshman center Francis Chukwudebelu is listed at 6-10 but was not one of the main statistical drivers. The mismatch to attack is not necessarily height but vertical pop and brute-force post size at the 5. Oboye’s offensive efficiency is excellent, but if your center is bigger and more physical, you can make him guard length and avoid giving him easy rolls. Conversely, if your 4-man cannot defend in space, Mahi and Ensminger can pull that player into actions and create passing windows. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster))

Isolation versus team offense tendencies: public team pages do not provide exact isolation play-type percentages, so I cannot honestly claim a precise iso rate from the web sources I found. What can be stated specifically is that Santa Clara’s scoring distribution and assist totals indicate a team-offense lean rather than heliocentric isolation. Four players averaged at least 8.0 points, three averaged at least 11.6, and the team averaged 16.8 assists per game. Ensminger’s passing spikes, Mahi’s 9-assist game against San Diego on January 4, and Gavalyugov’s 6-assist game in the March 9 win over Saint Mary’s all point to offense generated by drive-kick and extra passes rather than one player monopolizing creation. My inference is that late-clock possessions probably tilt more toward Hammond and Gavalyugov shot creation, but the offense overall is more collaborative than isolation-heavy. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Transition offense and defense frequency: exact frequency splits are not available in the public sources I could verify, so I cannot give a credible percentage for transition possession rate without inventing it. What I can state from the schedule and scoring logs is that Santa Clara is highly productive when games become open-floor affairs, as shown by 102 at Oregon State, 104 at LMU, 96 at Washington State, and 94 at San Francisco. Defensively, their season average of 72.4 points allowed is solid but not elite, and the biggest red flags come in track-meet losses: 98 allowed to New Mexico, 94 to Gonzaga at home, 89 at Gonzaga, and 86 at Saint Mary’s. That suggests their transition defense is most vulnerable after live-ball mistakes or long misses, especially against teams that can score before their length gets set. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/santa-clara/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Coaching adaptability: Herb Sendek’s staff does show evidence of adjustment across repeat opponents, though “mid-series” is more applicable to repeated conference matchups than a true playoff series. Santa Clara lost to Saint Mary’s 86-67 on February 25, then beat Saint Mary’s 76-71 in the WCC semifinal on March 9, with Gavalyugov scoring 23 and the Broncos surviving a much tighter, more controlled game. They also played Gonzaga much more competitively over time: down 89-77 on January 8, then within striking distance late in a 94-86 loss on February 14, then leading early in the WCC title game before falling 79-68 on March 10. That is not proof of universal tactical mastery, but it is concrete evidence that the staff can alter matchup plans, especially against familiar WCC opponents. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2541/santa-clara-broncos))

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must do four things. First, pick up full court and make Santa Clara initiate offense at 20 seconds or less; North Texas and San Diego both pushed the Broncos to 21 turnovers, the highest total Santa Clara had all year. Second, run shooters off the line and make Oboye and Mahi finish through size instead of letting Hammond and Graves get rhythm threes; Santa Clara lost badly when three-point efficiency cratered, especially the 10-for-44 night at New Mexico. Third, win the defensive glass and refuse pace; if Santa Clara gets clean rebound outlets, their offense jumps into the 90s. Fourth, attack their defense with force in transition after steals or long rebounds, because their worst losses came when opponents scored before their half-court length got organized. If you let Santa Clara play comfortable, shared-possession offense with early threes and paint touches, they can beat you with balance. If you turn the game into a physical, low-clock, rebound-first contest and punish every live-ball turnover, you give yourself the clearest path. ([santaclarabroncos.com](https://santaclarabroncos.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))
